svg.title: Why Routing Method Sets the Payout
svg.desc: diagram id: diag-07-routing-payout-comparison; chapter number: 4; chart type: stacked_comparison; title: Why Routing Method Sets the Payout; subtitle: Divergent buyer payouts versus zip-level precision routing; total range: $6 to $250 per call; caption: Whoever owns the call tracking and routing layer owns the margin: divergent buyers rule out simultaneous dial, and zip-level routing lifted mortgage calls from $10 to up to $250.; assumptions note: The $10, $22 and $6 payouts are Adam of Ringba's example of buyers that should never share a simultaneous dial. The $10 to $250 lift is one Ringba mortgage client routing high home-value California zips. Duplicates run 5% to 25% of call flow and about 35% of people live outside their area code.; note: Sources: Ringba / Adam (ojcbZuG798w), Ringba / Jordan Soto (yFkULiyenzk, 0eCCbtHmCJE).; buckets: label: Low-paying buyer in a split; low: 6; high: 6; notes: Route by priority and weight, not simultaneous dial.; label: Mid-paying buyer in a split; low: 10; high: 10; notes: East Coast and West Coast buyers need geo-accurate routing, not area code.; label: Top-paying buyer in a split; low: 22; high: 22; notes: Cap new buyers at $2,000 for the first 2 weeks until they pay.; label: Zip-level premium mortgage call; low: 10; high: 250; notes: Premium zips sold to smarter buyers; the rest dumped on networks.
